newsitem.title: USA: NYC council says mulling selling Swiss bank stocks.
newsitem.headline: NYC council says mulling selling Swiss bank stocks.

text.p: The New York City Council on Wednesday said it was weighing whether to require the city's pensions to divest themselves of Swiss banks stocks if the Swiss government does not reach a pact with Holocaust victims.
"The pensions are an area we're exploring," said a City Council official, who declined to be named.

A spokesman for the city comptroller said the city owns stock in three Swiss banks: 262,800 shares of Credit Suisse Group, which were worth nearly $26 million, 56,700 shares of Swiss Bank Corp, which were valued at $10.8 million, and 22,800 shares of Union Bank, pegged at about $13.3 million.
The City Council official added that the only other business that he knew of that the city and pensions have with Swiss banks was overnight loans.
"Swiss banks are among the institutions with whom we deal," he said, adding that he did not yet know how sizeable these dealings were.
City Council Speaker Peter Vallone proposed a bill that would bar the city from depositing money in Swiss banks until the Swiss government set up a compensation fund for Holocaust victims.

He noted that the additional step of having the pension funds divest their Swiss bank stocks would only be taken if the Swiss government failed to reach an acceptable pact with the victims of the Holocaust. "If that would happen, this would not be necessary."

In addition to the actions taken by the New York City Council, New York city and state sent warnings to Switzerland on Wednesday that they would make it difficult for Swiss banks to do business in New York unless the Swiss created a fund to compensate Holocaust victims.

The head of the New York State assembly announced hearings to determine "under what circumstances may a foreign bank's license or certification be revoked." The president of the New York City council introduced a bill to bar city funds from being deposited in Swiss banks until a compensation fund was set up.

This is the first time the state and local government have entered the international controversy over whether Swiss banks failed to return millions of dollars deposited by Jews before and during the Second World War.

Negotiations between the Swiss government and the World Jewish Congress are in a delicate phase with the Swiss government having said it would contribute to such a fund but failing to say how much money would go into it. Several major elements have to be negotiated before such a fund can be created, sources close to the talks said.

Earlier this week, the Swiss ambassador to Washington, Carlo Jagmetti, resigned after it was revealed he had urged his government to "wage war" against the WJC and other Jewish groups calling for such a fund, although he also supported the idea of a one-time payment to silence Switzerland's critics.
Any restrictions slapped on the ability of Swiss banks to do business in New York could have major repercussions as Wall Street is a major hub for foreign banking.
